title: Not scattered, not stuck
hookLine: attention not scattered outward, not stuck inward
carry: neither flies off nor holds on

cards: There are two ways to lose an afternoon. One: forty tabs open, three conversations, half-watching a video, attention flying outward in every direction.
Two: stuck in your own head, replaying a comment from last week, or so absorbed in a pleasant daydream you forget to eat. One scatters, one sticks. The hundred and thirty-eighth discourse names both.
The Buddha gives a short instruction and goes into his dwelling. The monks, just as with the bhaddekaratta verse, go looking for Mahakaccana.

teach.b: Here's the Buddha's instruction, in paraphrase.

A monk should examine things so that his consciousness isn't scattered and spread out externally, isn't stuck internally, and, not clinging, isn't agitated. Then there's no more birth, aging and death. That's all.
He goes in. Mahakaccana unpacks it. Scattered outward is when the eye sees a form and consciousness follows its attractive look, tied to its pleasure, chained to it.
Same for sounds, smells, tastes, touches and ideas. That's the forty tabs.
Stuck inward is subtler. Someone reaches a calm, joyful meditative state and then gets attached to the joy of it, bound by its pleasure. Even good stillness can become a place to hide.
That's taking the body, feelings, perceptions, formations or consciousness as myself, and then being shaken when they change. Mahakaccana puts the middle in an unusual place.

Not halfway between busy and calm, but beyond both habits: attention that can go out to the world without being dragged away, and come home without being glued there. The Buddha, hearing it, approves.

Look back at the week: five messengers at Yama's court, one fine night, the verse explained, heirs of our deeds, more complex than it looks, two joys. And now a mind that neither flies off nor holds on.

how: Meditation teachers in many Buddhist schools warn both against distraction and against becoming attached to pleasant meditative states, and students are taught to notice each without forcing.

o: attention not dragged out or stuck inside
a mind that has emptied out every thought
focus held tight on one object all day

games.q: not scattered, not stuck: tap the pairs.
p: following the attractive look of things
attached to the joy of calm

s: in MN 138 being stuck inward can mean clinging to the joy of meditation
Mahakaccana says even a calm, joyful state can become something to cling to.
the Buddha explains the saying in full detail himself
he gives it briefly and goes inside; Mahakaccana explains it, and the Buddha approves.
the discourse says attention should never go outward
the trouble is being dragged away by attraction, not seeing the world at all.

games.q: you've reached a calm, joyful state in meditation, and you never want to leave it. in Mahakaccana's terms, what's happening?
o: consciousness is stuck inward, bound by the joy of it.
games.why: being bound to the pleasure of a meditative state is what Mahakaccana calls being stuck internally.

practice: Settle on the breath, and when attention flies out to a sound, a plan, a screen, notice: scattered, and gently come back.
When you find yourself sinking into a pleasant fog or circling one thought, notice: stuck, and gently open up again to the whole body, the room. Home isn't a cell; it's a doorway you can stand in.

wordCard.voice: Not scattered. Attention that isn't dragged outward by what it sees, and isn't stuck inward in its own calm. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali vikkhitta: scattered, distracted. the Buddha's saying: not scattered externally, not stuck internally.

carryVoice: Your line: neither flies off nor holds on. A week of discourses ends with a mind at ease in the doorway. That's day five hundred four.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 138, Uddesavibhanga Sutta (the exposition of a summary)
